info.name: InfraNest API
info.description: The public InfraNest API. Set `token` to an API token (My account → Developer) and `organization_id` to your organization. Docs: https://developers.infranest.io

item.name: Domains
item.description: Domains and contacts as InfraNest knows them. Registrar actions (register, renew, transfer) stay in the app.

item.name: Get registration requirements for an extension

request.description:
The extra fields a registrar needs to register a domain under `tld` (for example the nexus details some country extensions ask for) and the registration periods it offers. `credential_id` and `tld` are required; `unknown` is true when the registrar could not be asked, in which case it may still refuse.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: Check a domain before transferring it in

request.description:
Checks the usual reasons an inbound transfer fails for the domain given by `name` and `tld`, before you submit it. Optionally pass `credential_id` for the registrar that would receive it; counts toward your plan’s hourly domain-check limit.

Scope: `domains.read`

Advisor findings across all your domains, most urgent first, with one finding per cause naming every domain it affects.

Scope: `domains.read`

A summary of your domains: what needs your attention, what the next year of renewals costs in your base currency, and how the portfolio is protected.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: Plan a settings change across domains

request.description:
For each domain in `ids` (up to 500), who would carry out turning `setting` on or off (`value`, default true). Changes nothing; each setting is changed through its own endpoint.

Scope: `domains.read`

For each domain in `ids` (up to 200), the email protection plan for `mode` (`protect` or `no_mail`) and its `route`: `here`, `elsewhere` (records to copy to your DNS host), `reconnect`, `unchanged`, `refused` or `none` (no zone held). Changes nothing; apply it through each zone’s email protection endpoint.

Scope: `domains.read`

For each domain in `ids` (up to 200), the CAA plan and its `route`, as for the email protection plan. Changes nothing; apply it through each zone’s CAA protection endpoint, which checks the zone’s certificates first.

Scope: `domains.read`

Adds a domain held at a registrar InfraNest is not connected to; its registrar, dates, status and nameservers are read from the public registry, now and daily. Only `name` is accepted; it counts toward your plan’s domain limit, and a domain already in your organization is refused with 422.

Scope: `domains.write`

Your domains, paginated with `page` and `per_page` (up to 200), each with its tags, advisor issue count and who hosts its website and mail. Filter with `search`, `credential`, `tag`, `active`, `expiring_soon`, `autorenew_off`, `website`, `mail` or `archived` (archived domains are left out unless asked for). Registration orders that failed are not domains you hold and are left out too; pass `include_failed=1` to list them, and `meta.counts.failed` says how many there are. Sort with `sort` (`domain`, `registrar`, `expires`) and `dir`.

Scope: `domains.read`

One domain with its full details. A domain over your plan’s domain limit is locked and cannot be opened; stale renewal pricing is refreshed in the background.

Scope: `domains.read`

Updates what InfraNest keeps for the domain: `notes`, `serves_website`, `expected_issuers`, `nameservers`, `registrar_contacts`, pricing and `tag_ids`. Registration data such as the expiry date and auto-renew is not accepted here; returns the domain’s full details.

Scope: `domains.write`

Takes the domain out of your working list while keeping it, its costs and its links; it keeps syncing and stops counting toward your plan’s domain limit. Refused with 422 while the domain is still active at a connected registrar.

Scope: `domains.write`

Brings an archived domain back into your working list, where it counts toward your plan’s domain limit again. A domain that is not archived is returned unchanged.

Scope: `domains.write`

The contacts assigned to the domain, each with its role in `pivot.type`.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: Assign a contact to a domain

request.description:
Assigns one of your contacts (`contact_id`) to the domain as `registrant`, `admin`, `tech` or `billing`, replacing whoever held that role. Recorded in InfraNest only; nothing is sent to the registrar.

Scope: `domains.write`

item.name: Remove a contact from a domain

request.description:
Unassigns the contact from the domain in every role it held. The contact itself is kept.

Scope: `domains.write`

The registrar’s current prices for the domain’s extension, asked live. Answers 404 when no registrar connection is linked; `pricing` is null when the registrar does not allow price lookups with your key.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: List a domain’s running registrar actions

request.description:
The action currently running at the registrar for this domain, where the registrar reports one; `can_retry` says whether it can be retried. An empty list when no registrar is linked or the registrar does not offer this.

Scope: `domains.read`

Checks each of the domain’s nameservers now: whether it answers on port 53 and is authoritative, whether the nameservers agree with each other, and whether DNSSEC validates. Empty when the domain has no nameservers; the result is kept for the advisor.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: Get how a domain is set up

request.description:
Who hosts the domain’s DNS and whether its nameservers answer, its mail provider, and the servers, certificates, monitors and status pages behind its addresses. Based on the DNS zone InfraNest holds; a domain whose DNS is hosted elsewhere gets no website or email details.

Scope: `domains.read`

What the registry itself says about the domain: its status codes, created and updated dates, the source (RDAP or WHOIS) and an excerpt of the raw answer.

Scope: `domains.read`

The current advisor findings for one domain, taking into account what its registrar supports.

Scope: `domains.read`

Which registrar operations are available for this domain, given what its registrar and extension support, with a `reason` when something is unavailable.

Scope: `domains.read`

The registry’s raw answer for the domain (RDAP, or WHOIS where the registry has no RDAP) and the server that gave it — the same record as the registry record. Served from the last answer for up to six hours; add `refresh=1` to ask the registry now, which counts against your domain checks per hour. Answers 422 with a message when the registry gave no answer, and 429 with `Retry-After` when InfraNest is pacing its questions to that registry and cannot ask again yet.

Scope: `domains.read`

The 50 most recent audit-log entries for the domain and its manual cost items, newest first.

Scope: `domains.read`

Fetches the domain’s EPP (auth) code live from its registrar; InfraNest never stores it. Needs write access; answers 404 when no registrar is linked or the registrar cannot provide the code.

Scope: `domains.read`

Your organization’s contacts, paginated with `page` and `per_page` (up to 200), with their tags. Filter with `search` or `tag`, and sort with `sort` (`name`, `company`, `email`, `city`, `country`) and `dir`.

Scope: `domains.read`

Creates a contact you can assign to domains as registrant, admin, tech or billing contact, optionally tagged with `tag_ids`.

Scope: `domains.write`

One contact with the domains it is assigned to.

Scope: `domains.read`

Updates the contact and, when `tag_ids` is sent, its tags. Recorded in InfraNest only; nothing is sent to a registrar.

Scope: `domains.write`

Deletes the contact from your organization.

Scope: `domains.write`

The 200 most recent moves of domains to another registrar you have connected, newest first, each with its domain, source and target connection, and current state.

Scope: `domains.read`

item.name: DNS
item.description: Zones and records at your DNS providers, templates and dynamic IP sources. Record changes are recorded in the zone history and can be undone.

item.name: Plan moving records to another server

request.description:
Shows what moving A/AAAA records from one server to another would change: each record with its new value, the records left out and why, and the monitors that would follow. Send `from_server_id` or `record_ids`, and optionally `to_server_id`; changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Sync a zone from its provider

request.description:
Queues a fresh import of the zone’s records from its DNS provider and answers with `queued: true`. Refused with 422 for a zone with no linked provider connection; manual syncs are limited per hour by your plan.

Scope: `dns.write`

item.name: Download a zone as a BIND file

request.description:
Returns the zone’s records as a BIND master file, in plain text, as an attachment named after the zone. The export is recorded in your audit log.

Scope: `dns.read`

The 50 most recent audit-log entries for the zone and its records, deleted records included, newest first.

Scope: `dns.read`

The zone’s record changes from its last 50 operations, newest first, grouped by the operation that made each batch, each with whether it can still be undone or restored to. Also returns a merged timeline and how many days of changes your plan keeps.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Preview restoring a zone to an earlier point

request.description:
Shows what putting every record back the way it was just after the batch `batch_id` (required) would change. Changes nothing; answers 404 when that batch is not in the zone’s history.

Scope: `dns.read`

Undoes one recorded change (`change_id`) or every change in a batch (`batch_id`), even across zones, pushing each one to the DNS provider. A change whose record has changed since, or that a dynamic IP keeps up to date, is skipped with its reason; answers 404 when nothing matches.

Scope: `dns.write`

item.name: List outside changes to a zone

request.description:
Records changed at the DNS provider outside InfraNest that nobody has decided on yet, newest first, each with what the record was and is now. `writable` says whether your earlier value can be put back for this zone.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: List leftover records in a zone

request.description:
Records the zone appears to have outgrown, such as old verification codes, addresses that stopped answering and duplicates, each with its reason and evidence. `writable` is false when InfraNest cannot change records in this zone.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Compare stored records with live DNS

request.description:
Records whose stored value differs from what public resolvers last answered, each with both values, the likely cause and whether taking the live value is offered. Also returns the zone’s delegation state; changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Check whether an address left your fleet

request.description:
Says whether the `address` query parameter (required) belongs to one of your servers, or is an address one of your servers held and released. A record cannot be pointed at a released address.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Get what a zone’s records point at

request.description:
For each record in the zone, keyed by record id: what it points at (one of your servers, a recognised service, a connection or a released address) and what uses it, such as monitors, certificates and status pages. Records with neither are left out; `long_ttl` is the TTL above which InfraNest calls a TTL long.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Preview what a record value would point at

request.description:
Says what a record of the given `type` with the given `value` (both required) would point at, before you save it. `points_at` is null when nothing is recognised.

Scope: `dns.read`

Sets or clears a note on what the record is for (`label`, up to 120 characters; empty or null clears it). Kept in InfraNest only and never written to the DNS provider; a labelled record is never proposed as a leftover.

Scope: `dns.write`

Your servers that have an address, each with the IPv4 and IPv6 address an A or AAAA record should hold to reach it. Where a server holds a whole IPv6 block, `basis` says how the address was chosen.

Scope: `dns.read`

Your DNS zones, paginated with `page` and `per_page` (up to 200), each with its provider, record count, tags and delegation state. Filter with `search`, `credential`, `tag` or `status` (`active`, `stale`, `drift` for records changed at the provider, or `security`) and sort with `sort` (`zone`, `provider`, `records`, `synced`) and `dir`; `meta.counts` holds the totals.

Scope: `dns.read`

One zone with all its records, its provider connection, whether record changes can be pushed to the provider, its delegation and DNSSEC details, and findings such as records pointing at released addresses. Opening it may queue fresh nameserver and live-DNS checks in the background.

Scope: `dns.read`

Every record in the zone, ordered by type and name, with the dynamic IP source that keeps it up to date, if any. Filter by record type with `type`.

Scope: `dns.read`

Creates a record in the zone and pushes it to the DNS provider; `dry_run=1` returns the change without making it. Refused with 422 when the zone is read-only or an A/AAAA value is an address your fleet released, and with 409 when an apex CAA record would block a certificate’s renewal, unless `confirm_caa_impact` is sent.

Scope: `dns.write`

One record in the zone. Answers 404 when the record belongs to another zone.

Scope: `dns.read`

Changes the record and pushes the change to the DNS provider; `dry_run=1` returns the change without making it. Refused with 422 when the zone is read-only or a new A/AAAA value is an address your fleet released, and with 409 when an apex CAA change would block a certificate’s renewal, unless `confirm_caa_impact` is sent.

Scope: `dns.write`

Deletes the record at the DNS provider first, then in InfraNest; if the provider refuses, the record is kept and 502 is returned. Supports `dry_run=1`, and `confirm_caa_impact=1` after a 409 for an apex CAA record whose removal would block a certificate’s renewal.

Scope: `dns.write`

Your dynamic IP sources (connections whose address changes, such as a home or office line), ordered by label, each with its tags and the DNS records and firewalls it keeps up to date.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: List servers a dynamic IP can follow

request.description:
Your servers with an InfraNest agent, which a dynamic IP source can take its address from, most recent agent check-in first.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One source with its targets, its 20 most recent address events and the server agent it follows, if any. The update token is never included; `can_reveal` says whether it can be shown again.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Changes the `label`, whether an address change sends an alert (`alert_on_change`), and its tags (`tag_ids`, replacing them). The firewall settings `firewall_strict` and `firewall_fail_closed` decide who can reach a server and are not accepted from an API token.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Deletes the source; its update token stops working at once. The DNS records it kept up to date stay as they are. Refused for a source that keeps a firewall rule up to date — remove those in the app first.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Take the address from a server’s agent

request.description:
Makes the source follow the public address the InfraNest agent on `server_id` reports (a server from *List servers a dynamic IP can follow*), or stop following with `server_id: null`. Refused for a source that keeps a firewall rule up to date.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Get a dynamic IP source’s history

request.description:
Address changes, what each one updated or failed to update, and changes to the source’s settings, newest first. Drawn from your audit log, so it ages out with your plan’s audit retention.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Send the current address to every target again

request.description:
Re-applies the source’s current address to the DNS records and firewall rules it keeps up to date — after you fixed a record by hand, or after a provider refused an update. Changes no address. `applied` is how many targets were written.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Check in from your own address

request.description:
Sets the source’s address to the one this request comes from — for a script running on the connection itself, which need not know its address. Answers with the address and its family (`v4` or `v6`). Refused like setting the address for a source that keeps a firewall rule up to date.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Set a dynamic IP source’s address

request.description:
Sets the source’s current address to `ipv4` and/or `ipv6` (at least one) and updates the DNS records it keeps up to date, exactly as a router check-in would: the history, the change alert and the `dynamic_ip.changed` event follow. `changed` is false when the address was already this one. A source that keeps a firewall rule up to date answers 403 `not_token_writable`: use the app or the source’s own update URL. At most 60 calls a minute.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Keep a DNS record up to date with a source

request.description:
Attaches an existing A or AAAA record (`dns_record_id`), or creates one (`create`: `dns_zone_id`, `name`, `family` `v4` or `v6`), and sets it to the source’s current address. From then on every address change updates it. Firewall rules are attached in the app.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Stop keeping a DNS record up to date

request.description:
Detaches a DNS record from the source; the record keeps its current value. Detaching a firewall rule is refused for an API token.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

A summary across all your DNS zones: what needs your attention, grouped by cause, the recent changes, where your DNS is hosted and what is worth tidying up. Changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

Finds DNS records in any of your zones that match the `q` query parameter, by name, value or address, grouped by zone with the reason each one matched. A query shorter than two characters returns nothing with `too_short` set; at most 100 records are returned, with `truncated` set when there were more.

Scope: `dns.read`

The 200 most recent moves of a domain’s DNS to another DNS host, newest first, each with its domain, target connection, current `state` and timestamps.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Check a zone’s live DNS security

request.description:
Resolves the zone’s SPF, DMARC, DKIM, MX, CAA, MTA-STS, BIMI, NS, address and DNSSEC answers from public DNS right now, with findings judged by the same rules as the stored-record advisor. Reflects what the internet answers, not what InfraNest stores.

Scope: `dns.read`

Findings about the zone’s stored records, such as missing or weak email protection, with the snapshot those findings were judged from. Changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Preview email protection for a zone

request.description:
Shows each email record (such as SPF and DMARC) as it is and as it would be, or why a change is refused. `mode` is required: `protect` for a domain that receives mail, `no_mail` for one that sends none; `live=1` also checks against public DNS. Changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Preview CAA protection for a zone

request.description:
Shows the CAA records that would be added, each of the zone’s certificates and whether it stays renewable, or why a change is refused. `live=1` also checks each record against public DNS. Changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

Reads the zone’s DNSSEC state from its DNS provider, including the DS details to add at your registrar when signing is waiting on that step. `status` is null when the provider cannot sign the zone or its state could not be read.

Scope: `dns.read`

Asks public DNS resolvers for the record and reports, per resolver, whether its stored value is live yet; `tier=fast` uses only the quicker resolvers. With `landing=1` it instead reports whether the record’s latest change (or the one in `change_id`) has taken effect, and `landing` is null when nothing changed recently.

Scope: `dns.read`

The built-in DNS templates followed by your organization’s custom templates, each with its records, plus the TTL values a template can use.

Scope: `dns.read`

Shows each of the template’s records for the zone with its status (such as `add`, `overwrite` or `unchanged`), the existing value it would replace and the TTL the zone will actually get. `templateKey` is a built-in template’s slug or a custom template’s id; changes nothing.

Scope: `dns.read`

item.name: Apply a template to a zone

request.description:
Creates or updates the template’s records in the zone and pushes each change to the DNS provider; with `overwrite=false`, records that already exist with the same type and name are left alone. `dry_run=1` returns the changes without making any. A CAA record that would block a certificate’s renewal is refused with 409 unless `confirm_caa_impact` is sent.

Scope: `dns.write`

item.name: Certificates
item.description: TLS certificates InfraNest tracks or issues, and when they expire.

item.name: Preview domains to add from certificates

request.description:
The domain names your certificates use that InfraNest does not track yet, where each is registered as far as is known, and the certificates that use it. Also says how many more domains your plan allows; nothing is changed.

Scope: `domains.read`

Every TLS certificate in the organization, expired and expiring first, each with its health, findings and who renews it. Narrow it with `domain_id` or `monitoring_check_id`; the list is not paginated.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

For each of your domains, whether a certificate covers it (`covered`, `expiring`, `expired` or `uncovered`) and the best certificate that does. Superseded and dismissed certificates are left out.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Everything InfraNest found about your certificates that may need attention, from problems to recommendations, with counts per tier.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

An address-by-address view of the certificates your visitors actually receive, grouped by domain, with a summary, what needs you, the renewals due in the next 90 days and recommendations. Also lists the members who can be made a certificate’s owner.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Makes the member given in `user_id` the owner of each certificate in `certificate_ids` (up to 200). Refused when that person is not a member of the organization.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Preview monitors to add for certificates

request.description:
The addresses InfraNest suggests watching with an SSL monitor, the monitor each would get and the certificates involved. Also says how many more monitors your plan allows; nothing is changed.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The certificate recommendations already acted on, newest first: monitors and domains added from a recommendation and CAA records added to unblock a renewal, with who did it and when.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One certificate with its domain, server, monitor, owner and tags, where it is served and its place in the renewal series. Also includes its findings and whether its files can be fetched from the provider.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Changes InfraNest’s record of the certificate: owner, notes, subscription end date, seller, tags and any corrections to how it is classified (purpose, trust, validation, managed, renewal type). Only the fields you send change; `owner_user_id` must be a member of the organization.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Get a certificate’s files from the provider

request.description:
Asks the provider the certificate came from for its files and returns the files; each fetch is recorded in your audit log. Requires write access, and is refused when the certificate did not come from a connected provider that can hand files back or is not linked to a domain.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The certificate’s history across its renewals: when it was issued, renewed and expired, plus the changes recorded in your audit log. For certificates you renew and pay for yourself, it also marks the day to order the renewal and when the subscription ends.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Sets the yearly price InfraNest counts for this certificate, with optional currency and billing interval. Send an empty price to go back to the provider’s figure.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Sets the certificate aside so it no longer counts towards domain coverage. Send `dismissed: false` to restore it.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Preview the CAA fix for a certificate

request.description:
The exact CAA record that would let this certificate’s authority issue it again, the DNS zone it would go in, the CAA records already there and any other certificate it would block. Refused when the certificate’s CAA policy does not block its renewal; nothing is changed.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Servers and cloud
item.description: Servers, volumes, networks, firewalls and load balancers. Provider actions stay in the app; tokens edit InfraNest's own records and alerting.

request.description:
What needs you across your servers, one entry per cause with every server it affects and, in `prevention`, the automation recipe that would keep the cause from coming back and whether you already run it; what your cloud resources cost this month against six months ago and which types moved most; what the savings finder could save; how many servers have backups, delete protection, the agent reporting, SSH limited and no reboot waiting; and a count of each kind of resource with the one thing worth knowing about it.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Cloud resources that cost money and do nothing — idle servers, volumes attached to nothing, addresses assigned to nothing, snapshots older than 90 days or of deleted servers, load balancers with no targets — and servers that could run one size smaller. Each comes with the evidence it rests on, what it costs a month and whether it can be acted on from InfraNest; `decided` lists the ones somebody chose to keep or be asked about later.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Check whether a server could be one size smaller

request.description:
Judged on the highest CPU, memory and load the monitoring agent saw over the last 30 days, moved onto the next size down at the same provider: suggested only when every peak stays under 60% of the smaller size and its disk is no smaller. `status` says why when it is not suggested — no agent, not enough data, too busy, a disk that cannot shrink, or already the smallest size.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get the quietest hour for servers

request.description:
The quietest hour of the day for the servers in `server_ids` (one, or a group), from the last 30 days of the agent’s readings — or the provider’s CPU graph without the agent — read in `timezone`. Each hour carries its usual load and a level (`quiet`, `normal`, `busy`); `recommended_at` is the next occurrence of the quietest hour. With too few readings, `source` is `default` and the hour is the stated default. Pass `at` to judge one time.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Reboots and address moves waiting for the time they were scheduled for, and those that ran, failed or were cancelled in the last seven days. Filter to one server with `server_id`. Schedule one by sending `run_at` to the reboot or address-move endpoint.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get a safe reboot, resize or snapshot-first action

request.description:
One safe reboot, or a rebuild or delete waiting for a snapshot, with every step and its status. Poll it while `status` is `queued` or `running`; `failed_step` and `error_code` say where and why it stopped. `by` names the person who started it; `via` is `automation` or `schedule` when nobody pressed it.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every server InfraNest tracks in the organization, a page at a time, with its provider, status, addresses and tags. Filter with `search`, `status`, `running`, `datacenter`, `tag`, `credential`, `provider` or `tracking=untracked`, and sort with `sort` and `dir`; self-managed machines are counted in `meta` but not listed.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One server with its volumes, tags, cost breakdown and what its provider lets InfraNest do with it. Also says whether it can be renamed and whether its monitoring agent’s readings are being refused.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Changes a server’s name, city, country or tags; only the fields you send change. A new name is sent to the cloud provider first and refused when the provider cannot rename servers, while the provider’s own facts (addresses, type, status) can only be edited on a self-managed server.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Hides the server from every list, cost and alert in InfraNest without touching it at the provider, where it keeps running. It no longer counts towards your plan, and tracking it again restores its history.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Get what refers to a server’s addresses

request.description:
The DNS records, firewall rules and monitors that name this server’s IPv4 or IPv6 address, with a total. Also lists the other servers a DNS record could be moved to, which is useful before deleting the server.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Sets a manual price for the server in InfraNest, with optional currency and billing interval. A manual price is no longer overwritten by the provider’s price at each sync; nothing changes at the provider.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Drops the manual price and goes back to the price last synced from the provider. Returns the server with its updated cost breakdown.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Overrides the monthly backup cost InfraNest counts for this server with `backup_price_monthly`, net of tax. Send `null` to go back to the provider’s price; the server’s base price is not affected.

Scope: `cloud.write`

CPU, disk and network figures asked live from the cloud provider. Pick the figures with `types` (default `cpu,disk,network`; `memory` and `filesystem` add memory and root disk space in bytes where the provider reports them) and set the window with `start`, `end` and `step` in seconds (default: the last hour at 60 seconds); refused when the server has no linked provider account. For a server created within the last hour whose provider has no readings yet, the series are empty and `no_data_yet` is `true`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List what runs on a server

request.description:
The agent's processes, systemd services and timers, and containers, as workloads: processes attached to the service or container the agent says they run under (`attributed` is `cgroup`), or, where it did not say, grouped by command and attached to the service they are named after (`attributed` is `name`); timers carry `last_run_at` and `next_run_at`. Each with memory, CPU where known, restarts in the last 24 hours (`restarts_24h`) and the last 7 days (`restarts_7d`; when `restarts_7d_capped` is true the count reached the 100 InfraNest keeps, so read it as "at least"), a 7-day hourly memory `trend` (oldest first, null where nothing was sampled) and `observations`: `failed`, `restart_loop`, `memory_leak` (grows and resets on restart) or `no_heartbeat` (a scheduled job of yours that no heartbeat monitor watches), each with a `certainty`. Problems come first. Needs the server's agent.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Compare a server's workloads with a week earlier

request.description:
Each workload's average memory (`memory_bytes`) and CPU (`cpu_percent`, the share of the whole machine) between `from` and `to` (ISO 8601; default the last 24 hours, at most 8 days), as `now`, and over the same hours a week earlier (`compared_with`), as `then`. Read from the hourly samples kept for 15 days, so a window that starts more than 8 days ago has nothing to compare with. A side is null when the workload was not sampled in that window; CPU is null for a service or container whose processes your agent did not place. Workloads are services, containers and the heaviest process groups, each with its `kind`, `key` and display `name`. A longer window is refused with `range_too_large`. Needs the server's agent.

Scope: `cloud.read`

CPU in 15-minute steps (`cpu`, average and peak per step, null where nothing was reported), the `events` on the same axis (deploys, changes, restarts, certificate renewals, scheduled job runs, alerts) and up to three `sentences` as copy keys: an unexpected restart, or a CPU episode well above the day's normal with the change just before it, or said to be unexplained. Needs the server's agent or provider metrics.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List what will happen to a server next

request.description:
By date: disks forecast to fill (per mount), memory, CPU or load reaching its alert threshold at the current trend, scheduled reboots, certificates it serves renewing or expiring, Ubuntu Pro lapsing and the operating system leaving support. Forecasts without an honest fit and operating systems without a known support date are left out.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List what happened on a server

request.description:
Everything that happened on this server between `from` and `to` (ISO 8601; default the last 24 hours, at most 31 days), oldest first: deploys and releases, changes to the server, its firewalls and the DNS records pointing at it, reboots and unexpected restarts, provider outages, certificate renewals, scheduled job runs (timers that run more than 24 times a day are left out), backups your cloud provider took (`backup`, at the provider's own time, once your server's backup list has been read) and alerts. Each has a `kind`, the time `at`, a `title` (text, or a copy key with parameters) and a `link` to it in the app. A longer window is refused with `range_too_large`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List what is unusual on a server

request.description:
What your server did in the last 24 hours that does not match its normal, in `findings`, biggest departure first. Normal is the server's own range over the 14 days before (`normal.low` and `normal.high`, the 10th and 90th percentile of its hourly averages); a finding is a run of 15-minute steps above `normal.line`, with its `from`, `to`, `peak`, whether it is `ongoing`, and the metric's 96 steps in `series`. Each finding says how sure the cause is in `certainty`: `known` (you confirmed it before, or a scheduled job ran just before the same hour on at least three of the last seven days), `likely` (one cause and a second piece of evidence agrees) or `together` (several causes, or one with nothing to back it, or none). `cause` is null whenever `certainty` is `together`; `candidates` lists what came in the half hour before (deploys, changes, reboots and restarts, provider outages, scheduled jobs, services that restarted or ran out of memory, traffic above its normal, and the mount that grew), `rejected` what lined up but you said was not it, and `evidence` the supporting facts as copy keys. `enough_history` is false, with no findings, until the server has three days of hourly history (`history_hours`).

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Replay a metric alert rule over 30 days

request.description:
What a metric rule (`metric`, `operator`, `threshold`, `duration_minutes`) would have done on this server over the last 30 days, replayed on the hourly rollup: the hourly `series` (average and peak), the effective `line` (load thresholds are per CPU core), the `peak`, and `would_fire` as a range — `at_least` from hours whose average crossed for the whole window, `at_most` from hours whose peak crossed (null for a `<` rule). `firings` lists them, flagging those inside a maintenance window, which are not counted. `pattern` is set when every firing starts at the same hour (`daily`) or the same weekday and hour (`weekly`), in the organization's timezone. Pass `default_id` / `override_id` from the rule to get `fired`, the incidents it actually raised. `available` is false for a metric with no hourly history (load 5/15, inodes, security updates). `suggested` offers a better threshold, in the rule’s own units, only where the month shows one: `cannotFire` when the line sits far above the highest normal hour, `tooOften` when the rule fired ten times or more. Otherwise it is null, and always before the server has 28 days of history (`history_days`, `min_history_days`). Hours inside maintenance are not counted as normal. `normal` says where the metric normally tops out across the server’s week: the highest hour’s 90th percentile (`high`) and which hour of the week it is (`hour_of_week`, 0 = Monday 00:00 UTC), or `ready` false with the `weeks` learned so far.

Scope: `cloud.read`

When the server last started, every restart its agent has reported with who or what asked for it (`infranest`, `automation`, `outside` or `unexpected`) and any monitor outage at the same time, whether it needs a reboot and since when, and the actions scheduled on it. Without the agent, `running_since` is null and only `created_at` is known.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get what a server listens on and what its firewalls let in

request.description:
Every port the server listens on, as its agent read it, and every port its firewall rules open, each with a `verdict`: `open_for_nothing` (a rule opens it and nothing listens), `only_private_peers` (open to everyone and only private addresses connect), `no_rule` (listening on every address with no firewall in front, where it should not be public), `exposed` (a database, Remote Desktop or SSH open to everyone), `expected`, `local` (loopback only), `unclear` (nothing listens on the host but that cannot prove it unused — containers, or a cut-short reading) or `rule_only` (no reading to judge with). `basis` is `agent` when a reading from the last day was judged and `rules` when only the rules are known; `reading.state` says why (`no_agent`, `too_old`, `off`, `failed`, `pending`, `stale` or `ok`). Peer counts are counts of distinct addresses by class, never the addresses. `guess` is the service usually found on a well-known port: a guess, never the program the agent saw. `new` is true for a port that started listening in the last seven days, after the agent's first reading; `listened_before_at` is set when a port came back after stopping within the week.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List the ports that started listening on a server this week

request.description:
Each port the server's agent saw start listening in the last seven days, measured against the agent's first reading of what listens there: a port that was already listening when the agent began is never new, and one that stopped and came back within the week is not either. Ports bound to loopback only are left out. Each has `first_seen_at`, `exposure` — how far it reaches, from its bind address and the firewall rules applied to the server: `everyone`, `no_firewall` (a public address with no firewall InfraNest sees in front of it), `limited`, `blocked`, `private` or `unknown` (a firewall is on whose rules are not known) — `level` (`critical`, `warning` or `info`), and `around`: deploys of a repository linked to the server, service units that started and restarts from 15 minutes before it was first seen to 2 minutes after. `guess` is the service usually found on a well-known port, never the program the agent saw. `decided` is set when someone marked the port as expected or set it aside; you make that decision with the attention decisions endpoint and the port's `key`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

What the server is, in `roles`: any of `web`, `database`, `cache`, `queue` (runs background jobs), `mail`, `dns`, `backup` (keeps other servers' backups) and `containers` (runs containers), in that order. InfraNest recognises it from what runs on the server — the services and processes its agent reports, and whether it runs containers — and from what it is connected to: your other servers connecting to it on a database or cache port, a load balancer sending it traffic, and the names pointing at it. `evidence` lists, per role, what gave it away (`source` is `workload` or `relation`, a relation with its `type`, `id`, `url` and, for a server connecting to it, the `ports`); evidence you may not read is left out. `recognised` is what InfraNest recognises now, as of `recognised_at`; `corrected` is what you said instead on the server's page (null when you have not), with `corrected_at` and `corrected_by`, and `source` says which of the two `roles` is. `allow_auto_reboot` is whether automations may reboot it although it is a database; `auto_reboot_held` is true when they may not.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get what a safe reboot of a server would do

request.description:
Before a safe reboot: `mode` is `safe` (it leaves a load balancer whose targets can be changed here), `plain` (no such load balancer — `reason` says which — or `server_down`: the others could not carry it, but the server is not serving anyway, so it is rebooted where it is) or `unavailable` (self-managed, no provider to ask). Lists each load balancer it is behind with the servers left to carry the traffic and whether each is healthy — by the load balancer’s own health check as well as the server’s status, agent and monitors where the provider reports one per target (`lb_health`; `judged_by` is `provider`, `signals` or, per load balancer, `mixed`) — `carry_now` and `carry_hours` (about what CPU they would run at without it, now and per hour in `timezone`), `blocked` when it cannot start now (`only_target`, `targets_unhealthy`, `no_headroom`), `group`: the other servers with a reboot waiting, for one at a time, and the dialog’s words: `provider_label` (the provider the reboot goes through), `monitors` (the names of the monitors it waits for) `reboot_required` (when the agent says a reboot is waiting: since when, the newer kernel, the reason) and `database` (the server is a database, so what uses it loses it while it reboots).

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List a server’s safe reboots, resizes and snapshot-first actions

request.description:
The safe reboots, resizes, and rebuilds or deletes that wait for a snapshot first, on this server that are running or finished in the last seven days, newest first. Each lists its steps with their status (`pending`, `running`, `done`, `skipped`, `failed`) and, for a failure, the step and a reason code.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get whether a snapshot can be taken before a risky action

request.description:
Whether a rebuild, resize or delete of this server can wait for a snapshot first (`available`, or `reason` why not: `plan`, `provider`, `no_progress`, `no_provider`), what keeping the snapshot costs a month at this account’s snapshot rate (an upper bound, from the disk size; null when there is no priced snapshot to read the rate from), and `always`: whether the organization takes one before every risky action.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get the sizes a server can be resized to

request.description:
Before a resize: whether it can be done here (`available`, or `reason` why not: `self_managed`, `no_provider`, `provider`, `catalogue`), the size the server has now (`current`, with the disk it really has), and every size its provider offers it (`targets`), each with its monthly price, the `difference` to today's price, whether its disk is larger (`disk_grows`), and `blocked: disk` when its disk is smaller than the server's — a disk never shrinks. `rules` is the provider's: `power_off` (it resizes a stopped machine only, so the server is shut down first and started after), `disk_optional` (the disk may stay as it is, which keeps a later move back down possible), `upgrade_only` (larger sizes only, with no way back). `steps` lists what the resize runs, and `limits` how long each wait may take.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The recent actions the cloud provider reports for this server, asked live. Empty when the provider account’s access does not cover it; refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The firewall attached to this server, read live from the cloud provider. Refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The backups the cloud provider holds for this server, asked live. Each read also keeps when each backup was taken, so the server's events (and its Metrics charts) can mark them. Empty when the provider account’s access does not cover it; refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The add-ons the cloud provider reports for this server, asked live. Empty when the provider account’s access does not cover it; refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List images available to a server

request.description:
The operating system images the cloud provider offers for this server, under `images`. Empty when the provider account’s access does not cover the catalogue; refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List ISOs available to a server

request.description:
The ISO images the cloud provider offers for this server’s type, under `isos`. Refused when the server has no linked provider account.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Brings an untracked server back into lists, costs and alerts, with its history, tags and alert rules intact. It counts towards your plan again, so it is refused when you have reached your server limit.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Every storage volume InfraNest tracks in the organization, a page at a time, with the server it is attached to. Filter with `search`, `attached`, `unattached`, `server_id`, `status`, `tag` or `credential`, and sort with `sort` and `dir`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One volume with its server, tags, what its provider allows and the provider’s size limits where known.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every cloud firewall InfraNest tracks in the organization, a page at a time (`per_page`, default 20), ordered by account and name. Each includes the entries a Dynamic IP keeps up to date in it.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One firewall with its rules, tags, Dynamic IP entries, what its provider allows and the protocols it accepts.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Compares the firewall’s rules in InfraNest with the rules live at the cloud provider and returns `drifted` with the provider’s rules. When the provider cannot be asked, `drifted` is false and `provider_rules` is null.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The built-in firewall templates and the custom templates your organization has saved, with their rules.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The rules a template would add to the given firewall, alongside how many rules the firewall has now. `templateKey` is a built-in template’s slug or a custom template’s id; nothing is changed.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every load balancer InfraNest tracks in the organization, a page at a time. Filter with `search`, `running`, `status`, `datacenter`, `tag` or `credential`, and sort with `sort` and `dir`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One load balancer with its tags and what its provider allows.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The IP addresses across your cloud accounts, with the server each is attached to. Where a provider cannot list addresses directly, the list is built from your servers and misses unattached addresses; those accounts are named in `server_derived_credentials`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every private network InfraNest tracks in the organization, ordered by name, with its tags. Not paginated.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One private network with its tags and what its provider allows.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every snapshot InfraNest tracks in the organization, a page at a time: of a server (`kind: server`, with the server it belongs to) or of a volume (`kind: volume`, with the volume, where the provider lists them). Filter with `server_id`, `volume_id`, `status`, `credential` or `search`, and sort with `sort` and `dir`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One snapshot with the server or volume it was taken from.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List servers with their latest metrics

request.description:
Every server in the organization with its latest CPU, memory, disk, load and network readings, its alert-rule counts and whether it is breaching, and `roles`: what each server is (see the server’s `role`), a page at a time. `normal_now` gives, for CPU, memory and load, the range the server normally sits in at this hour of the week (`low`, `typical`, `high`: its 10th, 50th and 90th percentile, and the `weeks` behind it); it is null until four weeks are learned, unless the range is borrowed from a peer named in `borrowed_from`. Monitored servers come first; filter with `search`, `credential`, `tag` or `status` (for example `breaching`, `norules`, `notreporting`, `monitored`).

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get a server’s stored metric series

request.description:
Time series InfraNest has stored for this server, as `[unix seconds, value]` pairs, oldest first, with the alert threshold that applies to each metric. Pick a comma-separated `metrics` list, then either a fixed `range` (`live`, `h1`, `h12`, `h24`, `d7`, `d30`; default `h24`) or your own window with `from` and `to` (ISO 8601) and optionally `resolution`: `raw` for every sample (kept for 48 hours, at most 48 hours per request) or `hour` for hourly averages (at most 92 days per request). Without `resolution`, raw samples are used when they still cover the window. A longer range is refused with `range_too_large`. Points are paged with `page` and `per_page` (up to 10,000, the default); `pagination` says how many points the window holds and `window` the range that was applied. `normal` gives each requested metric’s normal week: `hours` holds 168 entries, one per hour of the week starting Monday 00:00 UTC, each `[p10, p50, p90]` of that hour’s averages over up to 12 weeks (null for an hour with too little history). It stays empty until `weeks` reaches `min_weeks` (4), unless a peer server behind the same load balancer or with the same role lends its week — then `borrowed_from` names it. `learning_since` and `reset_reason` (`resize`, `reinstall`, `role` or `source`) say when and why the week started again. Maintenance windows, incident hours and a memory leak’s climb are not learned.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The latest state the monitoring agent reported from inside the server: disk mounts with forecasts, top processes, watched services, containers and ignored units. Also includes the agent’s own health, version status and whether alerts are currently quiet.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Gives one of the server’s reported containers a display name in InfraNest, identified by `container_id`. Returns the server’s full list of saved container names; each server has a cap on saved names.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Removes the display name saved for the container given in `container_id`. Returns the server’s remaining saved container names.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Get what needs attention on a server

request.description:
A short summary of the server: its uptime, whether alerts are quiet and until when, and the metric trend closest to crossing its alert threshold. Fields are null when there is nothing to say. `unusual` lists the last 24 hours’ runs of hours that were unusual for this server at that hour of the week, one per metric: `from`, `to`, `peak` and `peak_at`, the `normal` range (`low`, `typical`, `high`) it was judged against, the `weeks` behind it and, when the range is a peer’s, `borrowed_from`. They are never sent as alerts.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get a server’s security and setup checks

request.description:
Every check on the server: whether a firewall protects it, whether SSH, Remote Desktop or a database is open to everyone, whether a port is reachable that should not be (from what the agent reads listening), backups, snapshots, delete protection, monitoring and alert rules, and — when the agent reports — pending reboots and uptime. Each check has a `status` (`error`, `warn`, `info`, `agent` when it needs the agent, or `pass`) and the evidence behind it. The servers list and the attention list report the same checks.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get what depends on a server

request.description:
What runs on the server, by role: the domains, addresses and load balancers it serves, its certificates, the monitors, alert rules and status pages watching it, the firewalls and backups protecting it, its volumes, networks and extra IP addresses, the automations aimed at it, and its recent incidents and planned maintenance. Roles with nothing in them, or that your role may not read, are left out.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Silences the server’s alerts for `minutes` (5 to 1440) by creating a short maintenance window, and returns when it ends. Refused when your plan does not include maintenance windows.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Ends a snooze before it runs out. Scheduled maintenance windows are left alone, so the response says whether anything was ended and until when alerts are still quiet.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Stops a failed system service, named in `unit`, from raising alerts on this server, without silencing other service failures. Any name is accepted; returns the server’s list of ignored units.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Lets the service named in `unit` raise alerts again on this server; if it is still failed, it counts from now. Returns the remaining ignored units.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Turn on monitoring for a server

request.description:
Starts monitoring the server in InfraNest and returns how many monitored servers your plan allows and uses. Refused when you have reached that limit; repeating it on a monitored server changes nothing.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Turn off monitoring for a server

request.description:
Stops monitoring the server and frees its place in your plan’s monitored-server count. The server itself is not affected.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Get the latest monitoring agent release

request.description:
The current release of the InfraNest monitoring agent with its checksums, the install script URLs and the address the agent should report to. The answer is the same for every server.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The tokens the monitoring agent on this server can report with, newest first, with who created each and when it was last used. The token values themselves are never returned.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Every alert in the catalogue for this server, each marked as inherited from the organization, overridden here or not configured, with `fired_30d`: how many incidents it raised on this server in the last 30 days. Older standalone rules are listed apart. With `active=1` it returns only the rules actually being evaluated, as a flat list.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Changes the `operator`, `threshold`, `duration_minutes` or `is_active` of one of this server’s rules. Changing the operator or threshold clears any breach the rule was tracking; durations outside the allowed range, or shorter than your plan allows, are refused.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Reset or delete a server alert rule

request.description:
Removes the rule from this server. For an override, the organization’s default applies again; an older standalone rule is simply deleted.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Override an alert rule for a server

request.description:
Sets this server’s own version of an organization alert, identified by `default_id` or a catalogue `key`, with any of `operator`, `threshold`, `duration_minutes` and `is_active`. Send `is_active: false` to stop watching it on this server only; anything you leave out is copied from the organization default.

Scope: `cloud.write`

Brings an untracked address back so it is checked and shown again. Its certificates and monitor were never changed.

Scope: `cloud.write`

item.name: Get a volume’s checks and usage

request.description:
Whether the volume is attached to a server, and — when the agent runs on that server — how full it is and when it will be full at its current rate, by the mount point the volume is at. Each check has a `status` (`error`, `warn`, `info`, `agent` when it needs the agent, or `pass`) and the evidence behind it. `usage` is null when no agent reports the volume.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Whether the firewall is applied to any server, for providers where a firewall is applied to servers, and — where the agent reads what listens on those servers — whether a rule is open for nothing. Each check has a `status` and the evidence behind it. `rules` lists each inbound rule with its `verdict` across the servers it applies to (`in_use`, `open_for_nothing`, `unclear`, `any_port` or `rule_only`) and each server’s own answer.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get a load balancer’s checks and targets

request.description:
Whether the load balancer has services and targets, whether a target fails the provider’s health check, and — where a monitor watches the load balancer — which targets have no monitor of their own. `targets` lists each target as the server it is, with its health and whether a monitor watches it.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Whether the network has a subnet a server can join through, and whether any server is on it. Each check has a `status` and the evidence behind it.

Scope: `cloud.read`

What the monitor on this address knows: its status, 30-day uptime, response time, the certificate each probe location receives and where its alerts go. `monitor` is null when nothing watches the address.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The 20 most recent links you created to ask someone else to connect a provider account, newest first, with who requested each one. Filter with `provider` or `kind`; the response also gives how many days a new link stays valid.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Monitoring
item.description: Monitors, their results and uptime, and deploy markers.

item.name: Suggest external services you depend on

request.description:
The third-party services your own records say you depend on and you do not follow yet: your DNS zones and their MX, SPF, CNAME and verification TXT records, your connected integrations, your servers, your registered domains and the issuers of your certificates. Nothing is looked up and nothing is stored; each answer is worked out when you ask. Each suggestion has its `reasons` (the `signal` — `mx`, `spf`, `cname`, `txt`, `zone`, `integration`, `server`, `registrar` or `issuer` — and the record or resource it came from), whether InfraNest can read its status (`readable`), the catalogue entry to follow (`external_service_id`, null when the page is not in your catalogue yet: add it by its `status_url`), the components to follow (`component_ids`) and the resources of yours to link (`links`). A reason drawn from DNS records, a registration or an integration is shown only when you may read DNS, domains or integrations. `dismissed` lists the keys you dismissed (an advisor dismissal of type `external_service`, check `suggested`).

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Suggest the components of an external service you use

request.description:
For the service in `external_service_id`: the components you use, each with its `reasons` — a `kind` of use at the provider (`dns`, `proxy`, `server`, `registrar`, `certificates`, `load_balancer`, `api`) with how many you have or the region it is in, `probe` with the city an InfraNest probe checks your sites from, or `signal` with the record type that named the service. `dismissed` is true for a component you said not to offer again. Nothing is followed until you change your selection.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

A paginated list of your monitors with their type, target, interval, current status, 24-hour uptime, a 24-hour status chart (`uptime_chart_24h`, one status per hour) and the last 30 days (`bars_30d`, one entry per day with its date `d`, uptime `p` and colour `c`, ending yesterday, and for your own monitors `s`, the day’s status as the monitor’s own page draws it), plus status counts in `meta`. Filter with `search`, `type`, `kind` (`own` or `external`), `status`, `enabled` and `tag`, and sort with `sort` and `dir`; pass `all=true` for a plain unpaginated list of every monitor.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Creates a monitor and queues its first check. Pass `external_service_id` instead of a target to watch a third-party status page; a heartbeat monitor gets its own ping URL as its target. Refused when the monitor count, interval, check type or regions are beyond your plan.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

One monitor with its settings, alert channels, tags, dependencies, maintenance windows, the status pages it appears on, its 30 most recent results and the interval it actually runs at under your plan. A monitor that watches a third-party status page also carries `external_service` with its components (each with the `status` it reads as — `up`, `degraded` or `down` — and, where the page gives it, `vendor_status`, the provider's own word, such as `under_maintenance`), `uptime_90d`, and `provider_incidents`: the incidents open on that status page that touch the components the monitor follows, each with its `title`, the provider’s `vendor_status`, its `impact` (`up`, `degraded` or `down`), a `url` to the provider’s page, the `components` it names and the `updates` the provider posted, newest first. Each incident also carries its `key`, the provider’s own id for it (its title when the page gives none), which is what you send to say an incident does not affect you; `provider_verdicts` lists the incidents of that status page you said do not affect you, with the `keys` each covers, its `title`, who said so (`by`) and when (`at`), until the provider closes them. `provider_month` says, for this calendar month, how many `incidents` the provider had on the components the monitor follows, how many of them `reached` your own monitors (grouped under it, or failing while it lasted, among the monitors that sit behind that provider) and for how many `minutes`. `provider_probe` is what InfraNest's probes saw of the provider's open incident, when it names a place one of them stands in or near: `state` `confirmed` (one of your monitors behind the provider failed from there, named in `failing`) or `no_effect` (they were checked from there and all came back up), with the `place`, whether the probe is only `near` it (in the same country), how many monitors were `checked` and `since` when; null when there is no such incident, probe or check to go on.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Changes only the fields you send; keys inside `settings` are merged rather than replaced. Refused when a new interval, check type or set of regions is beyond your plan.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Permanently deletes the monitor. A monitor locked because it is over your plan’s limit cannot be deleted this way.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

The monitor’s check results, newest first. With `resolution=raw` (the default) each result is one check by one probe, filterable by `status`; for HTTP, API and keyword monitors it also says where the response time went, in milliseconds: `dns_ms`, `connect_ms`, `tls_ms`, `server_ms` (waiting for the first byte) and `download_ms`, null when the location did not measure them, and `response_bytes`, how big the answer’s body was (null for a HEAD request, or a location on an older version). Its `meta` holds what the check saw: a keyword check’s `page_bytes` and, when it failed, an `excerpt` of the page’s text (at most 512 bytes); a ping’s `sent`, `received`, `loss_pct` and `jitter_ms`; a DNS check’s `records` with their `ttl` and the `resolver` asked (null for the location’s own); a redirect check’s `hops`, each `url` (without its query) and `status`; a heartbeat’s `run_duration_ms` when the check-in sent `duration`. Individual results are kept for 3 days. With `resolution=hour` or `day` each row sums one hour or one day across probes: checks by outcome (`checks_up`, `checks_degraded` for slow checks, `checks_down` for failures), `up_percent` and the p50 and p95 response times, reaching back as far as your plan keeps history. Set the window with `from` and `to` (ISO 8601; default: everything kept for raw, the last 24 hours for hours, the last 30 days for days), narrow it to one probe `region`, and page with `page` and `per_page` (up to 500, default 50). A range longer than the resolution allows — 3 days raw, 31 days by hour, 366 days by day — is refused with `range_too_large`. `window` repeats the range that was applied.

item.name: Get a monitor’s uptime and response-time stats

request.description:

item.name: Get a monitor on one time axis

request.description:
For `period` `24h` or `7d` (hourly buckets) or `30d` or `90d` (daily): the bucket starts, an `overall` status per bucket (coloured by confirmed downtime, or `planned` when the only downtime in it was planned maintenance) and `overall_uptime` (the share of the period no confirmed, unplanned incident covered, the figure the app shows), a `lanes` entry per location with its statuses and `uptime` (the share of its checks that came back up), the type's `main` lane (`response` with p50/p95 in milliseconds for HTTP, API, keyword, port, ping and redirect monitors, plus a `summary` of the period's p50 and p95 weighted by the number of checks; `days_left` for SSL; null otherwise), `regions` (for response monitors, the same p50/p95 per location), `breakdown` (for HTTP, API and keyword monitors, where the time goes per location: the period's median `dns`, `connect`, `tls`, `server` and `download` time in milliseconds, with the number of `checks` behind them; empty until your monitor has been checked by a location that measures them), `events` on the same axis (deploys, changes to what the monitor watches, its incidents, its maintenance), `deploy_shift` for response monitors — what the newest successful deploy in the period did to response time per location: the `deploy`, the `minutes` compared on each side (up to an hour, shorter when the deploy is younger or followed another one sooner; null under 15 minutes or without a deploy), the `before` and `after` windows, and per location the `checks`, median (`p50`) and `p95` on each side with the `change` (`slower`, `faster` or `same` — a move of at least a quarter and 20 ms for the median, 50 ms for p95 — or `insufficient` under 10 checks a side) and its `percent` — `upcoming_maintenance` that will mute it in the next 30 days, and `provider_maintenance`: the planned maintenance a provider published on its status page that this monitor will see in the next 14 days — on a monitor that watches a third-party status page, maintenance on the components it follows; on any other, maintenance at the providers it sits behind — each with its `id`, `title`, `status` (`scheduled` or `in_progress`), `starts_at` and `ends_at` (null where the provider gave none), `url`, the `components` it names, the `subscription` that follows it, how many `monitors` silencing it would cover, whether it is `silenceable` (it has a start and an end) and `silenced_window_id` once you silenced it. A monitor that watches a third-party status page and follows up to 12 of its components also carries `components`: one lane per followed component, with its `id`, `name`, the worst status it had in each bucket (null before its history begins) and its `uptime`.

item.name: Get a monitor's locations and last 90 days

request.description:

Planned maintenance is left out of `pct` and `minutes_down`.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Get a monitor’s uptime and response times for a period

request.description:
Totals for one window: `uptime_percent` (the share of the time no confirmed outage covered, the figure the app shows), `up_percent` (the share of checks that came back up), checks by outcome, p50 and p95 response time in milliseconds, and the number and minutes of unplanned incidents. Pick `period` (`24h`, `7d`, `30d` or `90d`, default `24h`) or set `from` and `to` (ISO 8601, at most 366 days apart; longer is refused with `range_too_large`); the window starts on the hour `from` falls in. Pass `region` for one probe region, where `uptime_percent` is the share of checks that were up. Response times over more than one hour or probe are averaged from hourly figures, weighted by the number of checks, so they are close rather than exact. `uptime_percent` is null when nothing was measured.

item.name: Get a monitor’s uptime target and this month’s allowance

request.description:

item.name: Get who an outage alert would reach

item.name: Suggest what to link to an external service

request.description:

A monitor with an uptime target carries `uptime_target` and an `allowance`: the month’s `allowed_minutes`, `used_minutes`, `remaining_minutes`, the `projected_uptime_pct` and `projected_miss_on` at the pace so far, and a `status` (`met` or `missed` for a closed month; `on_track`, `at_risk` or `missed` for the current one). item.name: Get the current status of everything

request.description:
Everything in your organization as it stands right now, in one call: every monitor with its `status` (`up`, `down`, `degraded`, `paused` or `unknown`), when it was last checked and its 24-hour uptime; every server with its state, whether its agent is reporting (null when no agent is installed) and how many of its alert rules are breaching; the open incidents; the maintenance windows running now; and counts of each in `summary`. Pass `tag` (a tag ID) to narrow it to monitors and servers with that tag, their incidents, and maintenance that carries the tag or covers them. `servers` is null when the token has no Cloud scope or your role cannot see servers.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Get what is going on right now

request.description:
One answer for the top of a monitoring page: `state` is `down`, `degraded`, `maintenance`, `recovered` or `clear`, in that order of precedence. `problems` groups what is wrong by root cause, cause first: a server and the monitors on it are one problem, with the server as `cause` and the monitors in `affected`. A problem that fails from only some locations carries `regional`, and is degraded rather than down. Each problem also says what it breaks: `why` is why its first failing monitor fails (the monitor `type`, the reason `code` and `params`, else the probe’s `message`), `locations` names the probe locations its monitors fail from right now, `status_pages` lists your status pages that show one of its monitors, with those `components`, and `long_standing` is true once it has been open for more than 7 days. Anything in a running maintenance window, silenced, or held back because its parent is down is not a problem; `maintenance` lists the windows and what they mute. For an hour after an incident closes, `recovered` says what it was and how long it lasted; after that it moves to `last_problem`. `provider_outages` lists the providers you watch with a third-party status monitor that report a problem right now, with the monitors that sit behind each one: by a DNS zone or a proxied record at that provider, a server there, or what you linked to the status monitor yourself (`via` is `dns`, `proxy`, `server` or `linked`). A provider you run on but do not watch is listed too, with `subscription` null, while it has an open incident that is a major outage or that names a region one of your servers is in there, and only when something of yours sits behind it. A server is listed only when it is in a region the provider reports failing; when the provider names no region, every server you have there is listed and `regions_unnamed` is true. Those monitors, and the status monitor itself, are listed there rather than in `problems`; if any of them fail, the state is `degraded`, never `down`. Each provider outage carries `service_id` and `incident_keys`, the provider’s own ids for the incidents it is made of. An incident you said does not affect you is left out until the provider closes it, and an incident that touches only components you stopped following is left out for good; the monitors behind either are then ordinary monitors again, listed in `problems` when they fail and alerting on their own. `provider_quieted` lists both, so they can be taken back: `incidents` with who said so and when, and `unfollowed` with the component and its provider. Pass `subject` as `monitor:{id}`, `server:{id}` or `incident:{id}` to narrow it to one thing. Server causes need a Cloud scope.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: List the status page updates your providers’ outages would post

request.description:
One drafted status page update for each provider outage your monitors fail behind right now (the situation’s `provider_outages` where one of the `monitors` is down or degraded). The `message` names the provider as the cause, in your workspace’s language and timezone, and the components those monitors feed on your status pages, which `pages` lists. An outage gets no draft when none of your monitors behind it fail, when none of them is on a status page, when it has been going on for less than the minutes your incident status rule asks for, when you said it does not affect you, or once anybody has posted to the status page about any of those monitors’ incidents. `targets` lists every incident it is posted on, once per status page it names. To send it, post `status`, `message` and `every_page: true` to `POST /organizations/{organization}/incidents/{incident}/updates` with the draft’s `incident_id`; when `auto_post` is true, your workspace posts drafts without asking and this one is posted within a minute. Pass `group` to get only the outage with that group.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Get the map of what reaches what

request.description:
Your monitoring as a map, built only from what you already have in InfraNest. `nodes` are the visitors, every address a monitor watches, the load balancers and servers those addresses reach, and the servers they depend on; each has a `column` (0 visitors to 4 data), a `route` to its page and its `facts` (the monitors on an address, the firewalls applied to a server, how many of a load balancer’s targets your provider reports healthy). `edges` say how each link is known in `via`: `dns` (an A/AAAA record in your zones, or one CNAME inside them), `ip` (the monitor watches the address itself), `monitor` (the monitor’s server link), `load_balancer` (a target) or `agent` (connections the agent saw repeatedly, with their `ports`). Nothing is matched by name. Colours come from the situation: `problems` is the same list as the situation’s, and `paths` lists each broken path from the visitors to its cause. `replay.frames` gives the map at each moment of the window — `states` per node, the `causes`, the `broken` edges by index, and the edges that did not exist at that moment in `absent` — and `replay.events` the failures, recoveries and changes in it. A past moment is drawn as it was: `edges` also holds the links the window had that are gone now (a DNS record since moved, a server since taken out of a load balancer), and a node only such a link reaches carries `past: true`. Links are kept for 14 days from `replay.edges_since`; before it, or while it is null, a moment is drawn on today’s links. A past moment is coloured by the incidents open then, and a monitor that was slow, or failing from some places while others reached it, reads `degraded` there. Pass `hours` (1, 6 or 24) for a longer window, or `incident` to see only that incident’s path over its own span. Servers, load balancers and firewalls need a Cloud scope; links from DNS need a DNS scope. At most 150 addresses are drawn, failing ones first; `truncated` says when more exist.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The body of the monitoring Overview. Every figure covers your own monitors only: a subscription to a provider’s status page (a monitor with `external_service_id`) is left out of `monitors`, `days`, `month`, `key_monitors` and `locations`, and so are its incidents. `monitors` counts your enabled monitors and how many are up; `days`, the last 30 days across every enabled monitor (each day the mean uptime of the monitors measured that day as `p`, the number of unplanned incidents that started on it as `incidents`, and its colour: `red` if one of them was major or critical, `yellow` for any other, `grey` with no readings, otherwise `green`); `month`, the 30-day uptime, the number of unplanned incidents and the minutes down; `key_monitors`, the monitors on a status page (or, with none, the enabled monitors, worst first), at most eight, each with its 30 daily bars, uptime, its last 24 response times (`spark`) and its current response time; and `locations`, each probe location checking them, with how many of your monitors were checked from there in the last hour (`checking`) and how many fail from there now (`failing`); and `services`, the providers’ status pages you subscribe to: `total`, and in `problems` those reporting a problem now, down first, each with its `state`, the `provider` it speaks for (null for a page InfraNest does not recognise), how many things you linked to it by hand (`linked`) and your monitors that sit behind it (`monitors`, each with its `state` and `via`: `proxy`, `dns`, `server` or `linked`). Cached for two minutes.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

What will happen soon, soonest first: maintenance windows starting in the next 7 days (`maintenance`, with `until` and how many monitors and servers they mute), disks forecast to fill (`disk_full`, `at` is the forecast moment) and servers whose agent reports a reboot is required (`reboot`, `at` is when that began). At most 6 rows in `items`, the rest counted in `more`. Disks and reboots need a Cloud scope.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Your monitors, one row per registrable domain (`shop.example.nl` and `api.example.nl` are both `example.nl`); a monitor whose target is an address is grouped under its server (`type` `server`), and one with neither under `other`. Each group has its worst `state`, how many monitors it holds, how many are down or degraded, 24 hourly `bars` (the worst monitor in each hour, oldest first) and a `note`: the newest team note on an open incident in it, or null. Paused and silenced monitors are counted but do not set the state. Problem groups come first. Answers are up to a minute old.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: List monitors with their locations, 30 days and alert reach

request.description:
Every monitor except third-party status monitors, one row each, by name: its `state` and `since` when it last changed; `group`, the key it falls under by domain (`domain:example.nl`, else `server:{id}`, else `other`) and by server (`server:{id}` or `other`, with `server_name`); `locations`, the newest result from each probe location in the last 30 minutes; `bars`, its last 30 days, each with its uptime and `s`, the day as the monitor’s own page draws it (`up`, `degraded`, `down`, `planned`, or null with nothing measured); `uptime` over them; `hours`, its last 24 hours the same way, oldest first, the last one the hour in progress; `spark`, its median response per hour over the last 12 hours (null for an hour with none); `ms`, the newest response time if it was up; `regional`, true when it fails from some locations and not from others right now; `flapping`, true while it is in an unstable period; `cause`, for a monitor that is down or degraded, the server that took it down when that server is in trouble itself (an open server incident, or not running), otherwise null; and `alerts`: `state` (`ok`, `nobody` or `failing`), the alert `channels` by name and the `people` who take the status email. Answers are up to a minute old.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: List deploys for a monitor or server
