The deploys linked to one monitor (`monitor`) or server (`server`) between `from` and `to`; the window defaults to the 24 hours before `to`, which defaults to now. Also lists the repositories linked to it. Each deploy carries its `verification`: after a successful production deploy (the repository default branch, an environment GitHub or its name marks as production, or as the `production` setting of the repository says) its monitors are checked more often for an hour, then that hour is compared with the hour before it — `state` (`watching` until `until`, then `done`; `cut_at` when a newer deploy reached one of its monitors first and ended the window there for that monitor), `verdict` (`better`, `unchanged`, `worse` or `insufficient`; with `reason: plan_interval` and the plan interval in `plan_interval_seconds` when the plan check interval left too few checks for a verdict), a `summary` of the p95 response time and failure share, and per monitor and location the numbers on both sides. Returns `first: true` when there is no earlier deploy to compare with, and `unavailable: true` when GitHub could not say. `verification` says whether the deploy made its monitors worse, as in the deploy list.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One deploy and what followed it. `effects` lists what changed in the `window` minutes after it (30, 60, 240 or 1440; default 60) against as long before it, each line with its `source`: the agent (CPU, memory, services that restarted by themselves) or your monitors (p95 response time and the share of failed checks, per location, from at least 10 checks a side). `verification` is the stored verdict on the hour after the deploy, as in the deploy list; with the default window the lines for monitors are drawn from it. `servers` says, per linked server, which version it runs when your pipeline reported it through the deploy hook after the deploy began (`reported_current` for this deploy's commit or tag, `reported_other` with the `version` it still runs — reported, so a fact), and otherwise whether its agent saw something start with the deploy (`restarted`), saw nothing start (`not_restarted`, inferred), or cannot tell; `partial_rollout` is true when some got it and some did not, `partial_reported` when that comes from reported versions, and `rollout_inferred` when any line is inferred from restarts. `expected` is who marked the deploy's side effects as intended, and when (null until someone did): such a deploy is no longer named as the likely cause of the slowdowns and resource changes it explains. `redeploy` says whether the previous version can be redeployed from the page (`state` `available`, or why not: `not_allowed` until a link for these deploys allows it, `no_app`, `no_previous`, `release`, `not_github`), how (`rerun` of the previous workflow run, or a new GitHub `deployment`), the `previous` deploy, a `github_url` to do it by hand, and the `last` redeploy started from the page. `changes` lists the pull requests in it, each with a `suspicion` level (`likely`, `possible` or `unrelated`) and the reason, when something changed after the deploy.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Your deploy tokens, newest first, with their name, creator, the monitors each token applies to, whether a signature is required and when each token was last used. Token secrets are never returned.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

When your next “needs you” summary for this organization is due, how it is delivered, and a preview of up to 10 items it would contain. `receives` is false when you have turned the summary off, and `available` is false when it cannot be put together right now.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Incidents
item.description: Incidents: open, update and resolve them.

request.description:
A paginated list of your monitors’ incidents with their monitor, status, impact, latest update and who acknowledged each one, and `affected`: how many monitors, servers and status pages it took down, counted across the incidents grouped with it. Counts are in `meta`. `period` is `24h`, `7d` (default), `30d` or `all`; filter with `status` (`open`, `acked` or `resolved`) and `search`, or pass `incident` to fetch a single incident whatever its age.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The last 90 days of unplanned incidents: `count`, `downtime_seconds`, the median time to acknowledge (`median_notice_seconds`) and to resolve (`median_fix_seconds`), how many started within 30 minutes of a change to what failed (`after_change` of `after_change_of` checked, the most recent 100) and the most common kind of that change (`common_change`). `previous_count` is the number of unplanned incidents in the 90 days before, to compare with. Vendor incidents are counted apart in `not_yours`. Up to ten minutes old.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Changes an incident’s `title`, `status`, `impact`, `description` or `is_planned`. Setting `status` to `resolved` resolves an open incident, and any other status reopens a resolved one; incidents imported from a third-party status page cannot be edited. The incident it returns says `alerts_silenced` when it was recorded during a maintenance window that silences alerts: it counts as planned maintenance, and nobody was notified when it opened or resolved.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

The incident’s public status updates and internal team notes, plus the alert channels that were notified, deploys shortly before it began, who PagerDuty is paging, notes from PagerDuty and tickets opened for it. An update with `posted_automatically` was posted by InfraNest from the incident’s draft, because your workspace lets drafts post without asking. `status_draft` is the status page update this incident would post, ready for you to send with `POST …/updates`: `kind` is `opened` (the outage is real by your rule in `GET …/incident-status-rule` and nothing has been posted about it yet) or `resolved` (it recovered after an update was posted, and nobody has said it is over). It carries the `status` and `message` to send, the status `pages` and `components` it names, how long it has been down (`down_minutes`), from how many locations it was seen down (`locations_down` of `locations_checked`, null when the monitor has no per-location results) and whether your workspace posts it without asking (`auto_post`). `targets` lists where it is posted: once per status page it names, on an incident that page shows (`incident_id`, the `page_ids` showing it, and `notify_page_ids` when only some of those pages’ subscribers are told, because another update already reached the rest). For an outage across several monitors on different status pages, that is more than this incident. It is null for a blip, for an incident on no status page, for planned work and for a monitor behind a provider that reports its own outage.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Posts a public status update with a `status` and `message`, and moves the incident to that status (`resolved` resolves it). Status page subscribers are notified unless you send `notify_subscribers: false`; incidents imported from a third-party status page cannot be updated. To send the incident’s drafted update (its `status_draft`, or the provider outage draft sent on this incident), pass `every_page: true`: it is then posted on each of the draft’s `targets`, so every status page the draft names shows it and each page’s subscribers are told once. The response is the first update posted.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Get an incident’s cause, what it affected and how it unfolded

request.description:
One incident as a whole. `cause` is the server whose failure took the others down when one did in the same window, otherwise the incident’s own monitor or subject. `affected` lists the other monitors, servers and status pages it touched. `events` holds what InfraNest saw, each with `at`, `kind`, `source` and `params`: `failed` and `recovered` for each affected monitor or server (`grouped` when it was folded under this incident), `alerted` with the destinations an alert actually reached (one event per minute), `acknowledged` with who did, and `handed_over` with whom it was handed `to` and `by` whom. Combine it with the incident’s updates and with what changed before it for the full timeline. `status_pages` lists every status page showing an affected monitor, with those components. `prevention` names what would have helped, or is null: an automation recipe in `template` — being told of DNS changes after a likely DNS cause, verifying deploys after a likely deploy, or announcing incidents on a status page nobody updated — and `active` says whether you already run it. When the incident drafts its own status page update, a silent status page is answered with a setting instead: `template` is null and `setting` is `auto_post_drafts`, the `auto_post` switch of the incident status rule, so the drafted update is posted without asking. With that switch on, the announcement recipe does not post for an outage the drafted update already covers, so visitors read about it once. `hand_over_to` lists the teammates you could hand an open incident to, with `on_call` set for whoever PagerDuty is paging for it; it is empty once the incident is resolved, or when you may not hand it over. Server details need a Cloud scope.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The incident’s summary as InfraNest drafts it from what it recorded, in Markdown: what was down and for how long, what else it affected, the first failure, the alert, the acknowledgement and the recovery, the likely cause and the changes just before it, and what it was if someone said so. Written in `locale` (`en`, `nl`, `de` or `fr`; your own language by default), with times in your time zone. `summary` is the summary saved on the incident, or null; a monthly client report uses the saved one, or this draft.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Hand an incident over to a teammate

request.description:
Passes an open incident to the teammate in `user_id`: it is acknowledged as theirs, they are told by a push notification or, when no push reaches them, by email, and the hand over appears on the incident’s timeline. An incident nobody had acknowledged is acknowledged by you first. The teammate must be able to act on incidents in this workspace; `story` lists who qualifies in `hand_over_to`. Returns the incident with who has it now.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Get when incidents draft status page updates

request.description:
When an incident drafts a status page update: once its monitor has been down for `min_minutes` from at least `min_locations` locations (or from every location it checks from, when that is fewer). `auto_post` is true when the drafts are posted without asking, with "resolved" posted when the monitor recovers. Unless you change it in the app, 3 minutes, 2 locations and never posted without asking.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Marks the incident as acknowledged by you, so your team knows someone is on it, and returns it with who acknowledged it.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Clears the acknowledgement so the incident reads as unhandled again.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Add a team note to an incident

request.description:
Adds an internal note in `body` for your team. Notes never appear on a status page.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Maintenance
item.description: Planned maintenance windows, which pause alerts and show on status pages.

request.description:
Changes the fields you send. Sending `check_ids` or `server_ids` replaces what the window covers, and an empty list clears it. Sending `public_notice` as null or empty takes the window off your status pages.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Permanently deletes the maintenance window.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Mark a maintenance window as verifying

request.description:
Moves a window that is in progress to `verifying`, while you check that everything works again. Refused for a window in any other state.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Marks a window that is in progress or verifying as completed. Refused for a window in any other state.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

A paginated list of your maintenance windows with the monitors, servers and tags each window covers, whether each window is in effect and its current or next occurrence, plus counts in `meta`. Filter with `search`, `tag` and `status` (`active`, `scheduled`, `recurring` or `completed`), and sort with `sort` (`schedule`, `name`, `monitors` or `status`) and `dir`.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Schedules maintenance for the monitors in `check_ids` and servers in `server_ids`; a window with no monitors applies to every monitor. A one-time window needs `starts_at` and `ends_at`, a `daily` or `weekly` one needs `start_time` and `duration_minutes`, and alerts are suppressed during it unless `suppress_alerts` is false. Status pages and their subscribers see only `public_notice`, the text written for the public, and only on the pages whose monitors the window covers, from a week before a one-time window starts until it ends. Send it empty or null to keep the window internal. Leave it out and the window stays internal too, unless your workspace posts drafted status updates without asking (`auto_post` in `GET …/incident-status-rule`): then it carries the notice drafted from what it covers, the one `GET …/maintenance-windows/notice-draft` returns, and the response shows it in `public_notice`. The name and description are never published.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Draft a maintenance window’s public notice

request.description:
The public notice a window covering the monitors in `check_ids` and the servers in `server_ids` would carry, written in your workspace’s language, and the status `pages` (with their `components`) it would appear on. With neither, the window covers every monitor, so every status page. `notice` is null when the window would appear on no status page. Nothing is saved: put the text in the window’s `public_notice` to publish it.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Status pages
item.description: Public status pages and what they show.

request.description:
Every status page in your organization with its component and subscriber counts, how many components are operational or degraded, which are down, and the page’s 90-day uptime. `component_feeds` says what feeds each component and what it shows now (`status`). `last_post` is what the page last told visitors: an incident `update` (with its `status`, and `automatic` when no person posted it) or an `announcement` (with its `title`), whichever is newer, or null.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One status page with its settings, its components with the monitor and group behind each, and counts of components, announcements and subscribers. `exclude_planned_downtime` says whether the page’s uptime figures leave planned maintenance out; when they do, the public page says so beside the figure. `uptime_target` is the uptime promised each calendar month across this page’s monitors (average), or null; `show_uptime_target` says whether the public page shows it. It is spent by the average of the monitors’ downtime, not the worst one’s, so it is not a promise that no monitor is ever down.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Get the internal view of a status page

request.description:
The team-only view of the page: each component with its monitor, runbook link, regions reporting and 30 days of uptime, plus active incidents, the next maintenance and the on-call note. When the page has an uptime target, `metrics.uptime_target` gives the current calendar month against it across this page’s monitors (average): `uptime_pct` and an `allowance` whose `used_minutes` is the average monitor’s downtime. These internal fields are never shown on the public page, and this view needs a plan that includes private status pages.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The page at a glance: setup (components, custom domain, subscribers, whether it is public), uptime over the page’s history window, current status with active incidents, and the next maintenance and announcement due to end.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Views, unique visitors and subscribe clicks over the last `days` (7, 30 or 90; default 30), compared with the period before, with the busiest day and a daily series. Counts only; no individual visits are recorded.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The page’s components in display order, each with its group, linked monitor and uptime bars over the page’s history window. A component with no monitor has no bars.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Add a component to a status page

request.description:
Adds a component with a `display_name`, optionally linked to one of your monitors with `monitoring_check_id`. A `group_name` that does not exist yet creates that group, and a `runbook_url` must start with https:// and is only shown internally.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Add several monitors to a status page

request.description:
Adds a component for each of up to 50 monitors in `monitoring_check_ids`, named after the monitor and optionally placed in `group_name`. Monitors already on the page are skipped and listed in `skipped`; third-party monitors are added ungrouped and do not affect the page’s overall status.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Changes the fields you send, such as the name, description, linked monitor, status override, group or runbook link. A new `group_name` creates that group.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: Remove a component from a status page

request.description:
Deletes the component from the page. The monitor behind it is not affected.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Sets the display order from `order`, a list of component IDs. Every ID must belong to this page.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

The page’s component groups in display order, each with how many components it holds.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Adds a group with a `name` at the end of the page. Names must be unique within the page.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Sets the display order from `order`, a list of group IDs. Every ID must belong to this page.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Renames the group for every component in it. Setting `shows_platform_status` to true on one group clears it from every other group on the page.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Removes the group but keeps its components, which become ungrouped. The response says how many were ungrouped.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

The announcements you posted on this page, newest first, including ones scheduled for later or no longer shown.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Publishes a notice with a `title` and `body` on the public page. `kind` is `information` or `warning`, and `show_from` and `show_until` limit when it is shown.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: List incidents and maintenance on a status page

request.description:
The incidents and maintenance windows that appear on this page automatically from its monitors, from the last 90 days or still open. Read-only; edit each one on the incident or maintenance window itself.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Changes the announcement’s title, body, kind or display window.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Removes the announcement from the page permanently.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

How many people subscribe to the page, how many have confirmed or are pending, a count per channel, and a 90-day growth curve. Counts only; use the subscriber list for individual entries.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The page’s subscribers, newest first, with their channel, label, confirmation date and whether delivery is failing. Filter with `q` (searches email addresses) and `status` (`confirmed` or `pending`), and page with `per_page` (10 to 100); reading the list is recorded in your audit log, and webhook addresses are never shown in full.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Whether the page’s custom domain, or the one in `domain`, sits in a DNS zone you manage in InfraNest, whether InfraNest can create the CNAME record there for you, and whether it is already published. Includes the CNAME target to point the domain at.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Alerts and notifications
item.description: Alert channels, alert rules and notification settings. Read only: changing who gets alerted stays in the app.

request.description:
Every place the organization sends alerts, such as email, Slack or Telegram, with how many checks use each and how many alerts it missed while it refused messages. Pass `personal=1` for only your own personal destinations.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One alert destination with the checks that send to it.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Automations
item.description: Automations and the connections they use. Read only.

request.description:
Every automation, newest first, with its tags and run statistics: runs in the last 30 and 7 days, success rate, average duration and the last run’s status. Test runs are not counted. `mode` is `act`, or `observe` for one that only records what it would have done, and `observed_30d` counts those records.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

One automation with its trigger, conditions, actions and tags, plus its 20 most recent runs and their steps.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The automation’s run history with each run’s steps, newest first, 25 per page. Filter with `status` and the dates `from` and `to`, and with `observed=1` for only the runs that recorded what the automation would have done. Unless you may edit automations, what triggered each run is left out and `details_hidden` is true.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The accounts automations can act through, such as GitHub, Jira or PagerDuty, with each one’s status, whether it is paused and whether its triggers can fire.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

item.name: Integrations
item.description: Connected providers and messaging apps. Read only: credentials are managed in the app.

request.description:
Every connected cloud, DNS, registrar and certificate account, with its health and how many zones, domains, certificates and servers it holds.

Scope: `cloud.read`

How many enabled provider accounts there are (`total`) and how many are currently degraded or down (`unhealthy`).

Scope: `cloud.read`

One connected provider account with its health, how many zones, domains, certificates and servers it holds, the registrar operations it supports and the result of its last permission check. Secrets are never returned.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: List a provider account’s call log

request.description:
The most recent 200 calls InfraNest made with this account, newest first. Filter with `status` (`success` or `failure`) and the dates `from` and `to`.

Scope: `cloud.read`

Everything the organization has connected — cloud, DNS, registrar and certificate accounts, alert destinations, outbound webhooks, automation connections and calendars — each with its status and health. A cloud, DNS, registrar or certificate account also carries `provider_status`: what the provider itself has wrong right now that concerns you — open incidents from its status page or feed, and failures InfraNest sees on its own calls to the provider across several workspaces — with `explains_failures` true when it is the provider’s API that is failing, so a failing account is the provider’s outage rather than its credential. It is null when nothing is wrong. Also returns summary counts and the integrations your plan does not include (`locks`).

Scope: `cloud.read`

Downloads every call logged for this integration as a CSV file, newest first. Takes the same `status`, `capability`, `direction`, `credential_id` and `search` filters as the activity list.

Scope: `cloud.read`

The calls made to and received from this integration, newest first, paginated with `per_page` (5 to 100, default 20). Filter with `status` (`success` or `error`), `capability`, `direction`, `credential_id` and `search`; `meta` lists the accounts and filter values available.

Scope: `cloud.read`

One connected account of an integration, whatever kind it is, with its status and health. A provider account also carries `provider_status`, the same as in the list of integrations. Returns 404 when the account does not exist or does not belong to this integration and organization.

Scope: `cloud.read`

What the integration offers, the organization’s connections to it, and whether your plan allows connecting it. Returns 404 for an unknown integration.

Scope: `cloud.read`

item.name: Get the outbound webhook JSON Schema

request.description:
The JSON Schema of the payload InfraNest sends to your webhook endpoints, for tools that type a payload from a schema. Narrow it with `events[]`; with none, it covers every event. `events` lists every event you can name.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

The connected registrar accounts that can register a caught domain, by name, and whether each may race for it. Makes no calls to the registrars.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

The connected registrar accounts that can register a caught domain. With `tld`, each says whether it carries that extension and what it charges, and `requirements` lists what the extension asks of a registrant, or null when nothing is on file.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

item.name: Check whether you already hold a domain

request.description:
The domain in your organization matching `name` and `tld` (both required) that you hold or are registering, or null when there is none.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

Everything the Drop catch overview shows in one read: how many watches need you and why, how many are at each stage of expiry, how catching went over the last 90 days, the names expected to drop in the next 30 days, and changes that would improve your chances.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

How your watches ended over a window set with `days` (`30`, `90`, `365` or `all`; default `90`): counts of names caught, renewed by their owner, sent to auction and lost, why each was lost, what the catches cost, and one row per outcome, newest first.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

item.name: Get what a caught domain gets by default

request.description:
What InfraNest sets up on a domain the moment a watch catches it, unless the watch chose otherwise: `auto_renew`, a DNS template (`dns_template`, a custom template id or a built-in slug) applied to a zone at `dns_credential_id`, an uptime monitor once its DNS points at a website (`monitor`), and tracking the certificate it serves (`certificate`). `is_default` is true while the organization has not changed it. `dns_hosts` lists the connected DNS accounts that can host the zone of a domain registered anywhere. Change the default with `drop_catch_once_caught` on the organization, and a single watch's choice with `once_caught` on the watch (null follows the organization).

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

The Discover searches you saved in this organization, newest first: the word (`q`), the window (`within`: `today`, `7d` or `30d`), the longest name wanted (`max_length`, or null for any) and whether names with a bad reputation are hidden. `last_sent_at` and `last_sent_count` say when the morning email last sent new matches and how many. Only your own searches; nobody else in the organization sees them.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

Your watched domains, paginated with `per_page` (default 25, at most 200) and sorted with `sort` and `dir`. Filter with `search`, `tag` and flags such as `active`, `available`, `registered`, `failed`, `paused`, `in_auction`, `needs_you`, `drops_soon` and `no_backup`; `meta` carries counts per filter. Each watch carries a `reading`: its stage, when it is expected to drop and where that date comes from, how it will be caught, and its chances as a word with a reason.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

One watched domain with its stored WHOIS record, lifecycle dates, estimated drop date, the check schedule still ahead and drop statistics for its extension. It also carries its `reading` (the same one the list gives), `readiness` (the last "ready for the drop" check and when it ran), `registry_source` (how InfraNest checks the name and when the registry last answered), `let_go` (the signs that the owner is giving the name up, each with the date it was seen), `hears` (who is told about it: the watch's own `recipients`, or the organization's alert routing when `recipients` is null), `alerts_so_far` (how the organization's earlier alerts ended) and `self_registration` (where somebody registers it themselves when it comes free). Set `recipients` with a PATCH: `{people: [{user_id, email, app}], channels: [alert channel id]}`, or null to follow the organization again. `once_caught_applied` is what is set up on the domain once it is caught, and whose choice that is (`source`: `watch` or `organization`); set the watch's own with `once_caught` in a PATCH, or null to follow the organization. Once caught, `caught_setup` says what came of each step on the domain: `done`, `waiting`, `blocked` with a `reason`, or `off`.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

item.name: Get the options for registering a free watched domain

request.description:
What registering the watched domain by hand needs: `watch` (its name and whether it is free now), `registrars` (your connected registrar accounts that can register it, cheapest first, each with its price, `cheapest`, and `confirms_price`, whether it can check this name's own price before buying) and, when none is connected, `connectable` (the registrars you could connect for it; `sells` is true when one is known to sell the extension, null when not yet known). Register it with `POST domains/register`; on a plan without domain registration that is accepted for a watched domain that is free now.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

Every availability check run on the watched domain, newest first, 100 per page. Filter with `status`.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

Every attempt to register the watched domain, newest first, 50 per page.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

Changes detected in the watched domain’s WHOIS record, newest first, 50 per page.

Scope: `drop-catch.read`

item.name: Organization and members
item.description: The organizations a token can reach, their members, roles, single sign-on and dashboards. Read only.

request.description:
Every organization you are a member of, with your role and its member count. An organization that requires its own single sign-on, which this session has not used, is listed by name only.

Scope: `members.read`

The organization’s settings, with the name and email address of each member.

Scope: `members.read`

Every member of the organization with their role. `email_undeliverable` is true when email to that address can no longer be delivered.

Scope: `members.read`

Invitations that have not been accepted yet, with who sent each one and the role it grants.

Scope: `members.read`

Up to five matches per kind for `q` (at least 2 characters): domains, servers, DNS zones, monitors (by name or target), certificates, contacts, status pages, watched domains, load balancers, volumes, firewalls and dynamic IP sources. Each match has its `id`, a `label`, sometimes a `sublabel` (an address or target) and the `url` of its page in the app. A kind your token or role may not read is left out. `related`, when `q` is exactly one of your domains, lists what that domain is connected to.

The built-in roles followed by the organization’s custom roles, each with its permissions.

Scope: `members.read`

One role and its permissions. Either a built-in role or one of this organization’s custom roles.

Scope: `members.read`

Removes everything in your sandbox organization and restores its sample zones, records, monitors, server and tags. Works only on a sandbox, with its own test token or from the app; any other organization answers 404.

item.name: Tags and custom fields
item.description: Tags and custom fields, which work across every module.

request.description:
The organization’s custom field definitions in display order. Pass `entity_type` to list only the fields that apply to that kind of record.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Defines a custom field with `entity_types`, a unique `key`, a `label` and a `type`; select and multi-select fields also need `options`. Requires a plan that includes custom fields.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Replaces the field’s definition; send the full set of fields, as on create. Requires a plan that includes custom fields.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

Deletes the field definition together with every value stored for it. Requires a plan that includes custom fields.

Scope: `monitoring.write`

item.name: List custom field values for a record

request.description:
The custom field values set on one record. `entity_type` and `entity_id` are required; returns 404 when the record is not in this organization.

Scope: `monitoring.read`

Sets the `value` of one field (`definition_id`) on one record (`entity_type`, `entity_id`), checked against the field’s type and options. A null value clears it and returns 204. Requires a plan that includes custom fields.
